title: Cut UPFs to Prevent Heart Disease, Says Study
paragraphs: Eating fewer ultra-processed foods may help protect the heart, according to new research from the United States.

The study was led by Dr. Amier Haidar, a cardiology fellow at the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston. It was presented at a meeting of the American College of Cardiology in March 2026 and published in the journal JACC Advances. The researchers used data from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, which included 6,814 American adults aged between 45 and 84 who did not have heart disease when they joined the study. The participants answered questions about how many servings of different types of food they ate.

Ultra-processed foods are industrially made products that often contain added sugar, fat and salt. Examples include chips, crackers, frozen meals, processed meats, sugary drinks, breakfast cereals and many types of bread.

The researchers found that each additional daily serving of ultra-processed food was linked to a 5.1% higher risk of serious heart problems, such as heart attacks and strokes. People who ate the most ultra-processed food, about 9.3 servings a day on average, were 67% more likely to experience these problems or die from heart disease or stroke than those who ate the least, about one serving a day. Importantly, the link remained even after the researchers took into account total calories, overall diet quality and conditions such as diabetes and obesity.
The risk was higher among Black participants. The researchers believe that food marketing aimed at minorities and limited access to fresh food in some neighborhoods may play a role.

A separate study from Canada, published in 2026, found that among adults with high blood pressure or high cholesterol, eating 10% less ultra-processed food was linked to about a 13% lower risk of heart disease.

Haidar recommends reading nutrition labels and eating ultra-processed foods in moderation. However, the study relied on what people reported eating, and it shows a link rather than proving cause and effect.
